title: Least Squares and Best-Fit Lines (6.4-6.5)
description: Days 38-39: least squares as projection onto the column space, the normal equations, solving small examples, residuals, best-fit lines and curves, outliers, and QR. 12 questions pulled per attempt.

questions.prompt: When $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ has no solution, a **least-squares solution** $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is one that
choices: makes $\hat{\mathbf x}$ as short as possible
makes $\|\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}\|$ as small as possible
explanations: Length of $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is not what is minimized; it is the distance from $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ to $\mathbf b$.
There is no exact solution; least squares gives the closest we can get.
The dimensions do not even match in general; the condition involves $A^TA$.

questions.prompt: The closest point to $\mathbf b$ in the column space of $A$ is
choices: the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf b$ onto col$(A)$
explanations: $\mathbf 0$ is in col$(A)$ but is generally not the closest point.
The nearest point depends on all the columns, not just the first.
$\mathbf b$ is only in col$(A)$ when the system is consistent.

questions.prompt: If $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is a least-squares solution, the residual $\mathbf r=\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is
explanations: The residual need not be parallel to $\mathbf b$.
It is *perpendicular* to col$(A)$; it would be in the column space only if it were $\mathbf 0$.
It is zero only when $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is consistent.

questions.prompt: The normal equations for $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ are
explanations: $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is in $\mathbb R^m$ and $A^T\mathbf b$ is in $\mathbb R^n$.
The order is $A^TA$ (which is $n\times n$), and the right side is $A^T\mathbf b$.
Without the extra $A$ the sizes do not match: $A^T$ is $n\times m$ and $\hat{\mathbf x}$ has $n$ entries.

questions.prompt: The normal equations come from the fact that $A^T\mathbf r=\mathbf 0$ with $\mathbf r=\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}$. Substituting gives
explanations: The orthogonality condition uses $A^T$, not $A$.
$A^T\mathbf b$ is generally not zero.
That would force the system to be consistent.

questions.prompt: The normal equations are
choices: consistent only when $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is consistent
explanations: The projection of $\mathbf b$ always exists, so the normal equations always have a solution.
They always have at least one solution.
$A$ can be any shape.

questions.prompt: The least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is **unique** exactly when
choices: the columns of $A$ are linearly independent
explanations: More columns than rows forces dependent columns, so $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is not unique.
Consistency does not make $\hat{\mathbf x}$ unique; independence of columns does.
A square $A$ with dependent columns still has many solutions.

questions.prompt: If the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent, then the normal equations have
choices: infinitely many solutions, all with the same projection $A\hat{\mathbf x}$
explanations: $A^TA$ is singular, so the solution is not unique.
They are always consistent.
The projection of $\mathbf b$ is unique even when $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is not.

questions.prompt: If $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is consistent, then the least-squares solutions are
choices: exactly the exact solutions, and $\mathbf r=\mathbf 0$
explanations: An exact solution has residual $\mathbf 0$.
Least squares is still defined and agrees.
An exact solution makes $\|\mathbf b-A\mathbf x\|=0$, the smallest possible.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is $m\times n$, then $\hat{\mathbf x}$ lives in
choices: $\mathbb R^m$ and the projection in $\mathbb R^n$
$\mathbb R^n$ and the projection $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ lives in $\mathbb R^m$
$\mathbb R^m$ and the projection in $\mathbb R^m$
$\mathbb R^n$ and the projection in $\mathbb R^n$
explanations: Swapped: $\hat{\mathbf x}$ has one entry per column ($n$) and $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ has one per row ($m$).
$\hat{\mathbf x}$ has $n$ entries, one per column.
$A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is a combination of columns, which have $m$ entries.

questions.prompt: $A^TA$ is always
explanations: $A^TA$ is $n\times n$, not $m\times m$.
$A^TA$ and $AA^T$ have different sizes unless $A$ is square, and are generally different.
$(A^TA)^T=A^TA$ and its size is $n\times n$.

questions.prompt: $A^TA$ is invertible exactly when
choices: the columns of $A$ are linearly independent
explanations: Rows of $A$ being independent describes $AA^T$, not $A^TA$.
A non-square $A$ can still give an invertible $A^TA$.
$\mathbf b$ does not enter $A^TA$.

questions.prompt: The least-squares solution is the $\mathbf x$ that makes the **sum of the squares** of the entries of $\mathbf b-A\mathbf x$ smallest.
explanations: That is the definition: minimizing $\|\mathbf b-A\mathbf x\|$ is the same as minimizing the sum of squares.

questions.prompt: The residual vector of a least-squares solution lies in the column space of $A$.
explanations: It is perpendicular to the column space. It could lie in both only if it were $\mathbf 0$.

questions.prompt: The projection $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the same for every least-squares solution $\hat{\mathbf x}$.
explanations: It is the unique closest point of col$(A)$ to $\mathbf b$.

questions.prompt: To find a least-squares solution you can row reduce $[A\mid\mathbf b]$ directly.
explanations: If $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ is inconsistent, that matrix reduces to a contradiction. Row reduce $[A^TA\mid A^T\mathbf b]$ instead.

questions.prompt: If $\hat{\mathbf x}$ solves the normal equations, then $A^T(\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x})=\mathbf 0$.
explanations: That is just the normal equations rearranged.

questions.prompt: Least squares solves $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ exactly even when $\mathbf b$ is not in col$(A)$.
explanations: It can't: $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is the projection of $\mathbf b$, which differs from $\mathbf b$ unless $\mathbf b$ is in col$(A)$.

questions.prompt: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$. Then $A^TA=$
explanations: That is $A$ with a row removed, not $A^TA$. Compute dot products of the columns.
Column dot product $(1,0,1)\cdot(0,1,1)=1$, not $0$.
$A^TA$ is $2\times2$ here.

questions.prompt: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf b=(1,1,0)$, $A^T\mathbf b=$
explanations: $A^T\mathbf b$ is in $\mathbb R^2$, not $\mathbb R^3$.
Each entry is a column dotted with $\mathbf b$: $(1,0,1)\cdot(1,1,0)=1$.
$A^T\mathbf b=(1,1)$, not zero.

questions.prompt: Least squares for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf b=(1,1,0)$: $\hat{\mathbf x}=$
explanations: That is the first two entries of the residual, not $\hat{\mathbf x}$.
That would be $A^T\mathbf b$, not the solution of $A^TA\hat{\mathbf x}=A^T\mathbf b$.

questions.prompt: For the same problem the projection $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is
explanations: That is $\mathbf b$, which is not in col$(A)$.
That is $\hat{\mathbf x}$; multiply by $A$ to get the projection in $\mathbb R^3$.
That is the residual, not the projection.

questions.prompt: For the same problem the residual $\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is
explanations: The residual is $\mathbf 0$ only if the system is consistent; here $\mathbf b\notin$ col$(A)$.
That is $\mathbf b$.
That is the projection.

questions.prompt: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf b=(6,0,0)$. $A^TA=$
explanations: Second column dotted with first is $0+1+2=3$, not $2$.

questions.prompt: For that problem the least-squares solution is $\hat{\mathbf x}=$
explanations: Entries are swapped: the intercept is $5$ and the slope is $-3$.
That is $A^T\mathbf b$.
That gives $\|\mathbf b-A\mathbf x\|^2=8$, larger than the minimum $6$.

questions.prompt: For that problem the squared residual length $\|\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}\|^2$ is
explanations: The system is inconsistent, so the residual is not zero.
$8$ is the error for $\mathbf x=(4,-2)$, which is not the minimizer.
$36=\|\mathbf b\|^2$ is the error for $\mathbf x=\mathbf 0$.

questions.prompt: The residual for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf b=(6,0,0)$ is $\mathbf r=(1,-2,1)$. Which check confirms it is correct?
explanations: Then the projection would be $\mathbf 0$.
$\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf b=6\neq0$; the right test is against the columns of $A$.
$A\mathbf r$ is not even defined ($A$ is $3\times2$, $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$).

questions.prompt: To fit $y=a+bx$ to data, the design matrix $A$ has columns
choices: a column of ones and a column of the $x$-values
explanations: The $y$-values form $\mathbf b$, not a column of $A$.
That fits a parabola through the origin; a line needs the constant column.
The $y$-values are the right side $\mathbf b$.

questions.prompt: For the data $(1,2),(2,3),(3,5),(4,4)$, the right-hand side vector $\mathbf b$ for a line fit is
explanations: That is the $x$-column.
That is $A^T\mathbf b$.
That is the column of ones.
The lower right entry is $\sum x^2=30$.
The order is $[[n,\sum x],[\sum x,\sum x^2]]$.
The entry is $\sum x^2=1+4+9+16=30$, not $(\sum x)^2$.

questions.prompt: For those data, $A^T\mathbf b=$
explanations: The second entry is $\sum xy=39$.
The order is $(\sum y,\sum xy)$.

questions.prompt: The best-fit line for $(1,2),(2,3),(3,5),(4,4)$ is
explanations: Check: $\sum r$ would not be $0$.
That line is not the minimizer; check $A^T\mathbf r=\mathbf 0$.
Intercept and slope are swapped.

questions.prompt: For the least-squares line, the residuals $r_i=y_i-(a+bx_i)$ always satisfy
explanations: $\sum r_i=0$, because $\mathbf r$ is orthogonal to the column of ones.
$\sum r_i^2=0$ only when the line passes through every point.
Only when the data are exactly linear.

questions.prompt: Why is $\sum r_i=0$ for a least-squares line with an intercept?
choices: the line goes through the origin
$\mathbf r$ is orthogonal to the column of ones
explanations: This holds for any data set.
A line with an intercept does not have to pass through the origin.
$\mathbf r$ is orthogonal to the $x$-column too, not parallel.

questions.prompt: Fitting $y=a+bx$ to $(0,6),(1,0),(2,0)$ gives
explanations: With intercept $3$ the line misses $(0,6)$ by $3$ and the total squared error is larger than $6$; the normal equations give $(5,-3)$.
The data decrease, so the slope is negative.
That passes through $(0,6)$ but does not minimize the total squared error.

questions.prompt: Adding one data point far from the others in $x$ and far from the line usually
choices: has no effect on the line
moves the least-squares line a lot
explanations: Squared residuals punish big misses, so the line tilts toward the outlier.
It makes the SSE larger.
It generally changes both slope and intercept.

questions.prompt: Least squares is sensitive to outliers because
choices: it minimizes squared residuals, which weight large errors heavily
explanations: That is a different method; least squares squares the errors.
Minimizing the largest error is minimax, a different fit.
It counts small errors too.

questions.prompt: To fit a parabola $y=c_0+c_1t+c_2t^2$ to data, the columns of $A$ are
explanations: $\mathbf y$ is $\mathbf b$, not a column of $A$.
Those fit a line.
That leaves out the constant term.

questions.prompt: Fitting a degree-4 polynomial to 5 data points with distinct $x$ values gives
choices: a worse fit than a line
a fit with SSE larger than a parabola
an exact fit (SSE $=0$) that may wiggle badly
explanations: More columns can only lower the SSE.
More columns can only lower the SSE.
The normal equations always have a solution.

questions.prompt: Going from a line to a parabola fit (adding the column $t^2$) can only
choices: lower or keep the same the sum of squared errors
explanations: The parabolas include all lines (take $c_2=0$), so the minimum cannot go up.
$A^TA$ gets bigger (another row and column).
It usually lowers it.

questions.prompt: When software solves least squares, it often uses $A=QR$ and then solves
explanations: Orders swapped.
$R$ is $n\times n$ and $\mathbf b$ is in $\mathbb R^m$; project with $Q^T$ first.
$Q^T$ must multiply both sides.

questions.prompt: Using $A=QR$: $A^TA\hat{\mathbf x}=A^T\mathbf b$ simplifies to $R^TR\hat{\mathbf x}=R^TQ^T\mathbf b$, so (since $R$ is invertible)
explanations: $Q$ is not square in general.
Not dimensionally sensible.
Multiply by $R^{-1}$, not $R$.

Same $A$. The entry in row 1, column 1 of $A^TA$.
Same $A$ and $\mathbf b$: the **first entry** of $\hat{\mathbf x}$ (a fraction like 1/3 is fine).
Same problem: the **third entry** of the projection $A\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Same problem: the **third entry** of the residual $\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}$.
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf b=(6,0,0)$. The row 2, column 2 entry of $A^TA$.
Same $A$ and $\mathbf b$: the **second entry** of $A^T\mathbf b$.
Same problem: the **second entry** of $\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Same problem: the **third entry** of the projection $A\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Same problem: $\|\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}\|^2$.
Same data: $\sum xy=$

Same data: the **intercept** of the best-fit line.
Same data: the predicted $y$ at $x=3$.
Same data: the residual at $x=3$ (observed minus predicted).
Same data: the SSE (sum of squared residuals).

The design matrix for a **parabola** fit to 7 data points has how many columns?

A least-squares solution makes $A\hat{\mathbf x}$ the _____ of $\mathbf b$ onto col$(A)$.
questions.explanation: The closest point of a subspace is the orthogonal projection.

questions.prompt: The residual $\mathbf b-A\hat{\mathbf x}$ is _____ to the columns of $A$.
The equations $A^TA\hat{\mathbf x}=A^T\mathbf b$ are called the _____ equations.
questions.explanation: "Normal" refers to the residual being normal (perpendicular) to the column space.

questions.prompt: $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is unique when the columns of $A$ are linearly _____.
The sum of squared residuals is abbreviated _____.
In a line fit, the column of ones makes the residuals _____ to zero.
A point far from the others in $x$ that also misses the line has high _____ and can tilt the fit.
questions.explanation: Extreme-$x$ points act on a long lever arm.

questions.prompt: Fitting too many columns so that the curve passes through every point but predicts badly is called _____.
In $A=QR$, the matrix $R$ is _____ triangular.
The least-squares problem is also described as finding the _____ solution to an inconsistent system.
questions.explanation: The projection is the closest point.
